A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same goal recognition design framework, simulation domains, and human studies despite the changed title and formatting. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

before.justification: Sections 5.1–5.2 report original grid-world and Overcooked-AI simulations and human-subject experiments. Appendices A–B provide additional experimental results.

after.justification: V3 retains the original simulations and human studies and reports additional timing and ablation results in Tables 1, 2, and 4.

M1.justification: Appendix A.1 changes the reported predictor architecture from a custom convolution/pooling network to a ResNet18 backbone with a dense output head. This revises one component of the retained learned-oracle, Lagrangian-relaxation, and discrete-gradient optimization framework.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate 6x6 and 13x13 grid worlds, single-agent Overcooked-AI, optimal and hyperbolically discounted behavior, and human navigation. The new ablations remain within existing domains and budget scenarios; proposed future extensions are not evaluated.

E2.justification: The four search baselines and their participation in retained benchmarks remain unchanged. V3's ablation comparisons additionally evaluate linear and Transformer predictors against CNN configurations, coupled with greedy and proposed optimization. Newly discussed GRD methods such as Au and Pozanco are not added as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: The reported oracle dataset changes from 150K to 100K examples, retaining the 80/20 split, while simulation evaluation increases from 200 to at least 500 environments. V3 also introduces structured architecture/data-size ablation protocols and fixed-budget timing comparisons. These reported changes do not establish that every retained plot was rerun.

E4.justification: V3 adds systematic component ablations absent from v2. Section 5.1.1 and Appendix B.3 examine predictor architecture, 1K/10K/100K dataset sizes, and gradient versus greedy optimization across three modification settings and two grid sizes, including configurations where the proposed method underperforms.

E5.justification: V3 explicitly labels standard errors in Table 1 and reports additional ± values in the ablation tables. Section 5.2 adds a paired t-test with p < 0.005 for human overlapping actions, whereas v2 reported that comparison without this test. No new seed or repeated-training run counts are specified.

E6.justification: New timing and ablation tables substantially expand the results. For example, Table 2 reports 13x13 CNN-based reductions of 8.6/10.4/10.8 versus true-wcd greedy's 7.6/9.2/9.8 for standard/individual/shared settings. V2 Figure 6 becomes v3 Figure 5b with revised means and error bars. Most other plots and human prediction accuracies are retained; these changes do not establish a fixed-setting version-to-version performance gain.

T1.justification: The MDP and policy definitions, discounting formulas, constrained wcd objective, and Lagrangian remain unchanged. V3 clarifies the metric description and explains greedy behavior at budget one, but introduces no substantively new mathematical formulation, derivation, or proof.

C1.justification: The central claims concerning efficiency, general agent behavior, flexible constraints, and human validation remain. V3's conclusion adds a specific claim that predictive-oracle accuracy and expressiveness strongly affect environment-optimization quality, based on the new ablations.

C2.justification: V3 adds explanations involving budget allocation and greedy myopia, and interprets mixed small-grid ablations as evidence that advantages depend on environment complexity. Section 6 substantially expands limitations concerning data requirements and single-agent/discrete scope, alongside specific manipulation, privacy, and autonomy risks and possible mitigations.

D1.justification: Appendices A.1, B.2, and E add learning-rate choices, dense-head specifications, the explicit Lagrangian-multiplier grid and two-constraint combinations, and Python 3.10/PyTorch/autograd details. Participant payment and task duration are also newly specified. Hardware and simulation-generation instructions are retained; no new code or data release is reported.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands positioning within human-behavior modeling and heuristic GRD, including explicit discussion of Pozanco et al. (2024) and Au (2024). Additional citations support future directions and Bayesian inference, while the Feng et al. (2018) auction citation is removed.

P1.justification: The title changes and prose is extensively rewritten across the introduction, related work, experimental discussion, and conclusion. Former numbered simulation scenarios become paragraph headings, the ablation study occupies Section 5.1.1, and appendices gain B.2, B.3, and E. Terminology is standardized around GRD.

P2.justification: V3 changes typography and figure placement, adds three tables, transposes the human prediction-accuracy table, and combines v2 Figures 5–6 into v3 Figure 5a–b. Appendix runtime panels change from a 2x2 arrangement to one row, and the learning curve is resized beside text. These are substantial display changes beyond renumbering.

improvement.justification: V3 improves assessability through component ablations, explicit multiplier settings, and clearer data and applicability limitations. The ablations expose benefits and small-grid failures that v2 did not analyze. Gains remain limited: Table 1 leaves its fixed budgets unspecified and reports higher mean runtime than predicted-wcd greedy in three of four settings, so the broad efficiency narrative still needs qualification.
